clue.text: Is Keir Starmer like a household appliance?

definitions.text: Is Keir Starmer like a household appliance?

blocks.note: surface reading: a gadget such as a dishwasher that spares effort around the home
setter's reading: the leader of a political party, pictured as rescuing that party

explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer leads Britain's Labour Party, so the question asks whether he is rescuing it; the phrase also describes appliances that spare effort.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishwashers and washing machines are described as devices that reduce the effort of housework, and the phrase also reads as rescuing a party.

clue.text: Guard toilet, king not there

blocks.note: loo is an informal British word for a toilet
K is the chess abbreviation for king
someone who is out is not there

explanation.surface: A sentry is posted by the toilet while the king is away.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry posted to watch for danger is called this, a noun for a person keeping watch.

clue.text: Offer alien something in the bathroom

blocks.note: a bid is an offer at an auction
ET is the film extraterrestrial

explanation.surface: Someone offers a space visitor an item from the bathroom.
explanation.definitionFit: This low basin for washing is a fixture found beside the toilet in many homes, so a vague but fair description.

clue.text: No better copper to infiltrate underground

indicators.note: something ground is crushed and broken up, so the letters beside it are rearranged
to infiltrate is to slip inside, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: the word splits as under plus ground; the first part is taken as written
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A police officer goes undercover in the criminal underworld, and things get no better.
explanation.walkthrough: Underground splits into under plus ground: copper as policeman suggests a mole, but it is the metal CU.
explanation.definitionFit: An illness not cured is one where the patient is no better, so the adjective matches the phrase.

clue.text: See 1
Car bomb will explode finally within earshot

indicators.note: finally points at the closing letter of each of the three words before it

blocks.note: Audi is a German car make
the last letters of bomb, will and explode

explanation.surface: A car bomb is about to go off, close enough to be heard.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything that can be heard is close enough for the ear to catch it, matching the adjectival phrase.

clue.text: It's all in the head of one famous mother downing a ruinous drink

indicators.note: downing a drink means swallowing it, so one piece ends up inside another

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
Mary, mother of Jesus, is the most famous mother
gin is known as mother's ruin, and the a is kept

explanation.surface: A celebrated mother knocks back a drink, and it is all in her head.
explanation.walkthrough: Mother's ruin is an old British nickname for gin.
explanation.definitionFit: Something existing only in the mind, not reality, is said to be all in the head, an idiom matching the adjective.

clue.text: Pants tucked up into mega bra? Goodness!

indicators.note: something tucked into the words is concealed inside them, spread across the clue
in a down entry, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: letters running across mega, bra and the start of Goodness

explanation.surface: Someone stuffs underwear into an enormous bra and exclaims in surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants is British slang for rubbish, not underwear, despite the bra beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang pants means nonsense or worthless stuff, a synonym for rubbish.

clue.text: Happy end not quite come to pass

indicators.note: not quite complete means each word is cut short by its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A happy ending fails to materialise.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to pass is an old idiom for occurring, so both are verbs for taking place.

clue.text: Silly Mack did not annoy anyone

indicators.note: silly suggests letters behaving foolishly and falling out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
to harry is to harass or pester

explanation.surface: A daft man called Mack did not bother a single soul.
explanation.definitionFit: Every Tom, Dick and Harry is an idiom for ordinary people at random, meaning just about anybody.

clue.text: Hat for 13?

blocks.note: first meaning: a stiff flat-topped straw hat
second meaning: the sailor at 13 down is someone who goes about in boats

explanation.walkthrough: The straw hat is also traditionally worn on the river, so the two meanings sit together.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the name of a flat straw hat and a noun for a person who takes to the water in a vessel.

clue.text: American politician leaving note for innkeeper

indicators.note: a piece that is leaving goes away from the longer word, which loses those letters

blocks.note: a member of the US Republican Party
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A US politician leaves a message for the landlord of an inn.
explanation.walkthrough: Note looks like a written message, but it is a musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain the keeper of a pub is called by this title, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Was at home when Yeats created noise

indicators.note: something created is made up afresh, so the poet's name is rearranged

blocks.note: the Irish poet's name, taken as written
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: Someone was at home while the poet Yeats was making a racket.
explanation.definitionFit: To remain indoors rather than going out is a phrasal verb meaning stopping in at your house.

clue.text: Cathy's kinky island sailor

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters of the name are bent out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A woman called Cathy has an unconventional seafaring partner on an island.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who sails a pleasure boat with sails is a kind of sailor, an example of the general term.

clue.text: Told not right to be joyous

indicators.note: not right means the abbreviation for right is removed from the word

blocks.note: a story that is related has been told
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone is told they are wrong, yet stays happy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe someone filled with great happiness, so they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Quiet, fortunate and courageous

blocks.note: p is piano, the musical direction for quietly
a synonym

explanation.surface: A description of someone who is silent, lucky and brave.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with pluck shows spirit in the face of danger, so the adjectives are synonyms for bravery.

clue.text: Circular field left undone

indicators.note: something undone is untied and loose, so the letters fall out of their order

blocks.note: lea is a poetic word for a meadow
taken as written

explanation.surface: A round field has been abandoned and left in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: Circular looks like an adjective describing the field, but it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular is a printed notice handed out to many people, the same as a printed handout sheet.

clue.text: We hear how urinary infections start

indicators.note: we hear means the result is judged by its spoken sound

blocks.note: urinary and infections start with U and I, and those letters joined by and are said the same way

explanation.surface: A doctor explains how urinary infections begin.
explanation.walkthrough: We is the definition, though it reads as the subject of hear.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun for the speaker together with the listener is a plural first person, which is what the phrase spells out.

clue.text: Stays up playing, collecting 100 for the kitty

indicators.note: letters that are playing are messing about and moving out of order
collecting means gathering something in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: Late-night gamblers stay up and collect a hundred pounds for the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitty looks like a pool of money for the card game, but it is a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitty and pussycat are both affectionate names for a domestic cat, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Giving a nudge to pig whose heart is moved by a distressed 'oink'

indicators.note: a distressed thing is shaken and disturbed, so the letters of the sound are jumbled
the middle of the animal word is moved out and something else replaces it

blocks.note: taken as written; its middle letter is the heart
taken as written, the sound a pig makes

explanation.surface: Someone prods a pig, which gives an unhappy grunt.
explanation.definitionFit: To poke is to prod someone with a finger, so the present participle means prodding them.

clue.text: Tasmania, lacking a renewable energy

indicators.note: lacking something means it is missing, so a letter is taken away
something renewable is made over again, so the remaining letters are reworked

blocks.note: the Australian island state, taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tasmania is short of green power sources.
explanation.walkthrough: Renewable energy looks like one phrase about power supply, but renewable is the signal and energy alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is the physical endurance to keep going, a sense of the word energy.

clue.text: Pair bananas with initially cherries or tangy fruit

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and change order
initially points to the opening letter of each word that follows

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letters of cherries, or and tangy

explanation.surface: A fruit salad of two bananas with cherries or something sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: Bananas looks like one of the fruits, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: This soft orange stone fruit is one example of the general category of fruit.

clue.text: Rapidly oppose easy money

blocks.note: a synonym
to buck a trend is to resist it

explanation.surface: Someone quickly sets themselves against a get-rich-quick scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick profit made with little effort, often dishonestly, is called by this idiom.

clue.text: Take in some swabs or bandages

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is used, a run of letters within them

blocks.note: letters running across swabs, or and the start of bandages

explanation.surface: Swabs or bandages soak up blood from a wound.
explanation.definitionFit: To soak up a liquid is to draw it inside, a phrasal verb with the same meaning.

clue.text: Pile of spin?

blocks.note: taken as written, then read as s plus pin, with a tack (a small pin) standing in for the pin

explanation.walkthrough: Spin is not worked on as a whole: read it as S plus pin, and swap pin for its synonym tack.
explanation.definitionFit: A heap of things placed one on top of another is a synonym for a pile of them.

clue.text: Tailless bird is in shade — it's a pain in the neck!

indicators.note: a creature without a tail has lost its end, so the final letter goes
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: the pink wading bird
taken as written
a shade of meaning is a nuance

explanation.surface: A bird without a tail sits in the shade, making itself a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: Flaming is an old British intensifier, a mild swear word.
explanation.definitionFit: A pain in the neck is an idiom for an annoying person or thing, which this phrase describes emphatically.

clue.text: Seen at Wimbledon: new skincare tent

indicators.note: new suggests making the following letters over in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A new skincare tent has appeared at the Wimbledon championships.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon is the London lawn tennis championship.
explanation.definitionFit: Players at the famous lawn championship carry strung bats to hit the ball, so the definition describes an object present there.

clue.text: See 25
